*Owning buys control:* nobody else decides when you leave, what next year's rent is, or what color the walls are.
*Owning concentrates risk:* nearly all of the buyer's net worth is one house, one town, one roof.

items.text: How long will you stay? At today's national numbers, *under about nine years*, renting tends to win.
Find your price-to-rent ratio. At today's rates, around *14 or lower* breaks even in about five years. *18 or higher* doesn't break even in thirty.
Price in the full cost. Tax, insurance and maintenance added *40.6%* on top of the mortgage payment here.
Be honest about the habit. If you won't invest the difference, *buying wins much sooner*.

lines.text: Right now, the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced American home is $2,243.
And the typical rent on a single-family house? $2,243.
The same number. To the dollar.
So buying costs the same as renting, except you build equity. Easy decision, right?
Not even close. We built a model of both choices with this month's real data, and under typical assumptions, the renter stays richer than the buyer for over nine years.
But change one habit, and that number collapses to about two.
By the end of this video, you'll know the three numbers that decide your own breakeven year, and how to run them yourself.
When people compare renting to buying, they put the rent next to the mortgage payment. That's the tip of the iceberg.
Here's the full cost of owning that median home, in month one.
The mortgage: $2,243.
Property tax, at the national average effective rate of about 0.9%: another $313.
Homeowners insurance, now averaging around $3,000 a year: $251.
And maintenance: roofs, water heaters, the things nobody budgets for. Even at a conservative 1% of the home's value per year, that's $347 a month.
Total: $3,153. That's $910 a month more than renting a similar house.
And of that first mortgage payment, how much actually becomes equity?
Just $267.
The other $1,975 is interest. In month one, 88 cents of every mortgage dollar goes to the bank.
That's the key idea. Rent is money you'll never see again. But so are interest, property tax, insurance and maintenance.
Owning doesn't stop your money from disappearing. It just makes it disappear in more places.
To make this a fair fight, we gave two households exactly the same money.
The buyer puts 20% down, $83,340, plus about $8,300 in closing costs.
The renter doesn't buy, so they invest that same $91,674 instead.
Then, every single month, whoever has the cheaper housing invests the difference.
Today that's the renter, by $910 a month. But rent rises over time while the mortgage payment stays fixed, so eventually, it flips.
Here are the assumptions, all from this year's data.
Home values grow 4% a year, close to their long-run national average.
The renter's portfolio earns 7%, deliberately below the stock market's roughly 10% historical average.
When the buyer sells, they pay about 6% in commissions and fees.
And when the renter cashes out, they pay capital gains tax.
We left out the mortgage interest deduction. It helps some buyers, especially single filers, and would pull their breakeven earlier. That's one more reason to run your own numbers.
Here's the net worth of both households, meaning what each would walk away with if they sold everything that month.
On day one, the buyer is already behind. Closing costs are gone, and selling would cost another 6%. The buyer starts with about $58,000. The renter, $91,674.
After year one, the renter is still ahead by about $31,000.
Then the buyer starts closing the gap. Every year the home appreciates, the loan shrinks, and rent creeps up while the mortgage payment stays locked.
And at 9.4 years, the lines cross.
That's the breakeven. Sell before it, and renting would have left you richer. Stay past it, and buying pulls ahead, finishing thirty years about $143,000 richer: $1.3 million versus $1.15 million.
Zillow's own national estimate, using different assumptions, is 7.8 years. Same neighborhood.
So the rule isn't that buying always wins, or that renting is throwing money away. Buying is a bet that you'll stay long enough.
Now the honest part. 9.4 years is the answer for one set of assumptions. Change any of three numbers, and it moves a lot.
Lever one: how fast the home appreciates. At 4% a year, breakeven is 9.4 years.
At 5%, it drops to 4.6.
But at 3%, buying doesn't catch up within thirty years at all.
Lever two: your mortgage rate. At today's 7.11%, that's 9.4 years.
At 5%, just over three.
That's why a one-point drop in rates matters far more than it sounds.
Lever three is the big one: the price-to-rent ratio. Take a home's price, and divide it by a year of rent on a similar place. Nationally, right now, that's about 15.5.
Where it's 12, meaning homes are cheap relative to rent, buying breaks even in under three years.
Where it's 18 or higher, at today's rates, it doesn't break even within thirty years.
Put two of those levers together and you get the breakeven map. Mortgage rates run down the side, price-to-rent across the top.
Today's national numbers land right here: 9.4 years.
Lower rates or a lower price-to-rent, and buying wins fast. Move a column or two to the right, into pricier markets, and at today's rates it stops winning at all.
Now, the twist. Our renter is extremely disciplined. They invest every dollar they save, every month, for thirty years.
What if they don't? What if that $910 a month just gets spent?
Then buying breaks even in just 2.4 years, and never looks back.
This is the real reason so many homeowners end up wealthier than renters. It's not that a house is a magical investment.
It's that a mortgage is a forced savings plan, and most of us are bad at forcing ourselves.
One more honest caveat. Some of what matters most doesn't fit in a spreadsheet.
Renting buys flexibility. You can move for a better job in weeks, not months, and if local prices fall, that's your landlord's problem.
Owning buys control. Nobody else decides when you leave, what next year's rent will be, or what color the walls are.
And owning concentrates risk. In our model, nearly all of the buyer's net worth is one house, in one town, under one roof.
Put your own price on those, and weigh them alongside the math.
So, before you sign anything: how long will you really stay? At today's national numbers, under about nine years, renting tends to come out ahead.
Find your price-to-rent ratio. At today's rates, around 14 or lower breaks even in roughly five years. 18 or higher, not within thirty.
Price in the full cost. Here, tax, insurance and maintenance added 40.6% on top of the mortgage payment.
And be honest about the habit. If the difference won't get invested, buying wins much sooner.

And tell us your price-to-rent ratio in the comments. We'll model the most common ones in a follow-up.
